Senses.Explanation: Tiles breaking apart and ice melting away is a paired image for something collapsing and disappearing at once. Layman Pang says that a claimed branch of Shitou’s line breaks apart and melts away under examination. Yuanwu Keqin applies it to Devadatta’s skills; Tianyi Yihuai to an imagined gathering of Deshan, Linji, and the man from Caizhou; and Shishuang Chuyuan to a discussion involving Manjusri and Sudhana after Vimalakirti’s shout. Tiefu Zhisong and Yu’an Ji likewise use the whole paired predicate for the disappearance of what has just been assembled or asserted. The expression is not about literal roofing or ice.

Senses.Explanation: The Mirror of Qin is a named mirror repeatedly brought into Chan verse and exchange as an instrument before which a form, a speaking participant, or the person himself is exposed and distinguished. In the Recorded Sayings of Master Baiyu, Baiyu Jingsi says that before the mirror a jackal has no way to hide its original form; in the Recorded Sayings of Konggu Daocheng, Konggu Daocheng hangs the mirror at the head of a staff and says that every dust-mote land becomes responsive. In direct questioning recorded in the Recorded Sayings of Master Hansong, Hansong Zhicao answers after the absence of the mirror prompts the question how one can distinguish the matter. The compilers Jing and Yun, narrating Xuefeng Yicun's biography in the Zutang Collection, place Xuefeng face-to-face with the mirror and tell him to inspect himself. These are observable uses of the mirror in appraisal and exposure, not a claim that every mention carries one secret fixed meaning. The headword is repeatedly attested in the corpus.

Senses.PreferredTarget: alas, Buddha!
Senses.Explanation: “Alas, Buddha!” is an exclamatory response used to expose a speaker’s miss rather than a formal proposition about the Buddha. Xuedou Chongxian uses it after asking for one word that has broken out of delusion, and again as a substitute response when someone merely repeats the same thing. Dahui Zonggao exclaims it after a monk leaves smelling of the very confusion he failed to recognize. Faxi Yin says it when a monk answers from the top of the hundred-foot pole yet still cannot meet the raised bamboo slip. Yezhu Fuhui uses it when another master pauses and is caught before replying.
Senses.Note: The opening words exclaim distress or pity, and the final word directly addresses the Buddha. Preserve the abrupt vocative force.

Senses.Explanation: An imperative directing the addressed person or assembly to give close attention to what is about to be said or heard. Yangshan Huiji follows his declaration about the Great Vehicle with the doubled command “listen carefully, listen carefully” (摩訶衍法離四句絕百非。諦聽諦聽). Konggu Daocheng tells the assembly to “set your ears and listen carefully” (大眾！著耳諦聽), and Baiyu Jingsi says that anyone who has not yet seen must “listen carefully” (其或未見，更須諦聽). Luyuan answers an unnamed monk who asks for the purport with the command itself. In each use the first graph is adverbial: the cited passages command careful listening; they do not name an object called “the Truth.”
Senses.Note: The doubled imperative intensifies the same command. “Set your ears” is a supporting phrase in Konggu Daocheng’s turn, not a separate headword.

Senses.Explanation: Carefully observe the Teaching King’s teaching; the Teaching King’s teaching is thus is a fixed mallet formula at the close of a formal address. In the recorded sayings of Feiyin Tongrong and Baichi Xingyuan, an unnamed senior seat speaks it after the presiding teacher. Other records assign it to an unnamed white-hammer or closing-hammer officer. Complete Five Lamps instead places the same words in the Firm-Earth Deity’s praise. The grammatical speaker is therefore the named or unnamed mallet voice, not automatically the owner of the preceding address.
